newsitem.title: UK: Britain's FTSE on hold, awaits Labour tax news.
newsitem.headline: Britain's FTSE on hold, awaits Labour tax news.

text.p: British stocks defied expectations of a sharp fall on Friday in reaction to Labour's massive election win, opting to await government decisions on corporate and dividend taxes and interest rates.

The FTSE index of the top 100 companies was up 4.5 points at 4,449.5 by 1100 GMT, compared with expectations of a plunge of as much as 100 points if Labour won. The FTSE hit a session low of 4,423.6 in thin early trade.
"The FTSE at these levels is saying 'The election's over now let's get back to business as usual'," said one senior dealer at a major securities brokerage house.
"In fact, the market remains on hold, waiting to see if Labour have any ability to govern and what they are going to do on tax," he said.

Dealers and equity strategists said the unexpectedly large victory for Labour would increase fears of higher corporate taxes in the first budget. The new government's parliamentary majority will be about 180 seats.
"They are in an unbelievable position of power and as a group they have never run the country before. We are heading for a few months of mega uncertainty," a dealer said.
But several strategists said the FTSE was as likely to react to share price movements on Wall Street over the next few days as to decisions made by the new government.

"The City feels reassured that Labour have the same macro policies as the Conservatives," said NatWest Markets UK equity strategist Bob Semple. "The equity market as well as sterling and gilts (government bonds) were taking it calmly through the night.
"What we're going to face in the next few days and the next few months is concerns over tax risks," he said.

"The equity market looked like it was going to be weaker at the start because, although you can be relaxed about overall policy, there is plenty to worry about on detail such as corporate tax," he said.
The focus of tax concerns are how much the Labour government will levy a windfall tax on utilities and on tax credits on high dividend payers -- in particular utilities and financial stocks.
Utilities prices were expected to be marked two to three percent lower. Although they fell in early trading, losses were short-lived with no real selling pressure.

Severn Trent fell 6 pence a share to 750p, National Power 6p to 526-1/2p, Thames Water 6p to 673-1/2p and National Grid Plc fell 2p to 222-1/2p, BAA shed 3p to 512p, gas provider BG Plc a penny to 179-1/2p and Railtrack 12-1/2p to 449p.

"Utilities are on pretty attractive ratios, particularly the dividend yield and we will be looking at selected stocks which have a better chance of escaping the harshest levy of a windfall tax," said Andrew Stone, utilities analyst at Daiwa.
National Grid, privatised more recently, and Scottish power firms which do not enjoy what Labour calls excessive profitability are likely to fare best, Stone said.

Analysts are expecting a windfall tax of 3 billion to 10 billion pounds ($5 billion-$16 billion), with a range of 3-5 billion on electricity and water companies. They said utilities faced a couple of months of uncertainty while the market waited for Labour's first budget.
General tax and regulatory concerns were also likely to give investors a long-term bearish view on the sector, analysts said.

Banks were also marked down overnight on the prospect of a near-term interest rate rise after Labour's expected chancellor of the exchequer Gordon Brown said he would stick to an inflation target of 2.5 percent.
Barclays Bank shed 5-1/2p to 1,142-1/2p, Lloyds 5p to 800p and NatWest 4-1/2p to 722-1/2p.
The first meeting between the chancellor (finance minister) and the governor of the Bank of England, Eddie George, is set for May 7.
But the main hurdle for the equity market was expected to be Labour's first budget and the fear that it would hit the corporate sector hard.
"If it's two months before we see a budget, it will leave the market in a very moribund state," said James Dewhurst, equity salesman at Charterhouse Tilney.
"ACT (advance corporation taxation) is very significant. Every five percent drop in ACT equates to about 2.5 percent off the market," he said.

Under current legislation, pension funds are allowed to claim back ACT on dividends so any cut would reduce the dividend yield on individual shares. Mortgage interest relief and other corporate taxes may also come under scrutiny.
